title: Bucket over your head: how slow before it spills? 30 turns a minute on a 1 m arm
description:
Bucket over your head: how slow before it spills? A bucket of water on a 1 m arm (from the pivot at your shoulder to the water surface; the bucket's open top faces the pivot and the water fills it from 1.00 to 1.10 m) turns in a vertical circle at a steady rate: 36 turns a minute above, 21 below, the same arm and bucket, seen from the side with you at the pivot 1.5 m above the floor. The water is 25 parcels on a 5 by 5 grid. In the frame turning with the arm a parcel at radius rho feels omega^2 rho outward and g cos phi inward at phi from the top, so the bucket floor pushes it with N = m (omega^2 rho - g cos phi); a parcel leaves the moment N would go negative, on the way up, with the bucket's velocity, and then flies free under g (no air) until it hits the floor or you. The slow bucket is refilled at the bottom of each turn. Real time, 24 fast turns and 14 slow turns in 40 s; deterministic, no seed.

Measured:
- the surface water stays in while omega^2 r is at least g: the limit is omega = sqrt(g / r) = 3.132 rad/s = 29.9 turns a minute, one turn every 2.006 s; stepping whole rates through a turn, 29 rpm lets go 19.9 degrees before the top (the bucket would need to pull with 0.060 g at the top) and 30 rpm holds (0.006 g of push at the top), so 30 turns a minute is the slowest whole rate that holds
- 36 rpm: omega^2 r = 14.21 m/s^2; the bucket pushes on the surface water with 0.45 g at the top, 1.45 g at the sides and 2.45 g at the bottom; no parcel leaves
- 21 rpm: omega^2 r = 4.84 m/s^2; the push on the surface water reaches zero 60.5 degrees before the top (cos phi = omega^2 r / g = 0.493, 29.5 degrees above the horizontal); the water leaves at 2.20 m/s, rises to an apex 0.68 m above the pivot (0.36 m above your head) and comes down on your body 0.67 s later, 1.06 m above the floor; at the top the bucket would have had to pull with 0.51 g
- the 25 parcels leave between 60.5 and 57.2 degrees before the top over 0.026 s, at 2.20 to 2.43 m/s, and all of them come down on you within 0.54 to 0.82 s: 23 on the body, from 1.77 to 0.29 m above the floor, and 2 on the head; none reaches the floor and none meets the turning bucket again (closest 0.30 m)
- the stepped leave angles are within 2e-7 degrees of the closed form acos(omega^2 rho / g) and the velocity Verlet flights at 10,000 steps per second within 3e-13 m of the parabola
- other rates on the same arm: 15 rpm lets go 75 degrees before the top and the water lands on the floor 0.66 m short of you; 20 rpm lets go 63 degrees before the top and hits your shins; 24 rpm lets go 50 degrees before the top and lands on the floor 0.67 m past you; 26 rpm 41 degrees and 1.16 m past; 28 rpm 29 degrees and 1.72 m past; 29 rpm 20 degrees and 2.00 m past; 30 rpm and above hold

Why: the water stays in the bucket only while the bucket pushes on it. Going round a circle, the water needs a push toward the pivot of omega^2 r, more for a faster turn. At the top, gravity supplies g of that push for free, and the bucket floor supplies the rest. If omega^2 r is bigger than g, the bucket is pushing all the way round and the water rides along; at 36 turns a minute that push is 0.45 g at the top. If omega^2 r is smaller than g, gravity alone is already more than the circle needs before the bucket reaches the top: the push runs out, the water keeps going the way it was going while the bucket turns on without it, and gravity brings it down on you. The limit is where omega^2 r equals g: 30 turns a minute for a 1 m arm, one turn every two seconds. A longer arm may turn slower; the limit scales with the square root of the arm length.

Rerun sims/bucket/bucket.py with projects/bucket/manifest.json and you get these numbers exactly.

Made end to end by an AI agent: simulation, footage, voice, music, and edit.
